About this comparison +

A, B and C use the same character reference and image generator. E reuses A’s complete character artwork with an authored animation rig. D follows the same character brief using pixel-plugin’s drawing, animation and export tools in a locally built Aseprite. A–D use six transparent frames per action; E uses eight. The requested cameras and output frame sizes match within each view; generated camera angles can drift.

A follows Character Animation Creator’s pose and identity guidance, with its pixel cleanup and validation tools. B follows Pixel Art Agent Skill’s animation principles, fixed palette, atlas packing and pixel audit. A shared import step controls frame registration and jump height.

The moving ground shows the configured travel distance so you can inspect foot contact and sliding; it does not certify zero slip. The timeline exposes each retained frame and its duration. Phase numbers identify playback order; they do not certify correct leg alternation.

C uses Sprite-gen’s prompt templates, three-frame continuation chunks, green-screen removal and shared-scale processor through the app’s built-in image tool. This tests its workflow, not a different image model.

D uses explicitly authored pixel poses drawn through pixel-plugin’s bundled MCP server. Fixed templates preserve the head and body proportions; two alternating legs follow defined stance paths, running includes flight, and jumping follows a set height curve. The detail pass adds hair texture, face shading, finer glasses, shirt folds, denim seams and trainer details while retaining the original movement. Six-frame playback still has visible stepping and possible foot sliding between held frames.

E extends the Game Studio experiment with an authored animation rig. The original full-strip generation repeated the lead leg, while regenerated parts changed the character’s appearance. E now reuses A’s face, shirt, jeans, arms and trainers, with proportions measured separately for each view. Rotating joints, stable body artwork and explicit near/far overlap provide eight alternating poses per action. Native shirt texture backs the moving shoulders; full-length source limbs supply the foreshortened views. E’s eight-frame timeline shares cycle timing with A–D’s six-frame clips; each card displays its own frame. Travel follows the authored stance trajectory at sampled joints. Held frames still step, and rotated pixel textures can show angular edges. This is a hybrid correction using A’s art, not an independent Game Studio art sample.

This is a visual test of the five workflows, including the image generator’s variation. It is not a controlled ranking of different image models. A and B retain the previous registration corrections. C shows Sprite-gen’s own processing with a constant stage offset. Its retained frames still show inconsistent leg alternation; its processor centres jump poses and loses much of the jump arc. The RPG jump also drifts towards a three-quarter camera. Each view samples one direction; these are not full directional movement packs.
